recent_commits.message: Cache zip_peek() failures too, not just successes
recent_commits.body:
zip_peek()'s per-session cache only ever remembered a SUCCESS; a NULL
(host refused, rate-limited, or otherwise) was deliberately retried fresh
on every call, on the documented assumption that "a real 'not supported'
result would still return NULL again quickly."

That assumption holds for a host that plainly does not honour range
requests (a fast, clear refusal), but confirmed live 2026-09-09 to be false
when the host instead answers every call with a retryable-looking status
(403/429/5xx) persistently: a single zip_peek() call already pays
req_retry()'s full backoff sequence (up to 3 tries each, exponential up to
a 30s cap, across up to 3 separate HTTP calls this function and its
helpers make) before giving up. This file's own header comment already
documents that the SAME url is peeked more than once per pipeline run
(once in repo_check, again in download_repo_files()'s
.zip_fetch_members()) -- each call independently paying that cost again is
exactly what compounded a single persistently-403ing Zenodo archive
(SAPFLUXNET, 10.5281/zenodo.3971689, investigated the same day) into a
multi-hour stall, alongside the separate max_files_per_repo undercounting
bug fixed just before this.

Now caches a NULL result too (exists(url, envir=..., inherits=FALSE), not
mget's ifnotfound, so a cached failure is distinguishable from "never
attempted" -- confirmed live that assign(url, NULL, envir=...) really does
bind NULL in an environment, unlike env$x <- NULL on a list, which removes
the element). Trade-off: a transient failure that would have cleared by a
LATER call in the same session is no longer retried fresh either -- judged
acceptable, since the alternative (repeating a costly multi-minute retry
sequence every time the same URL is touched again) is what caused this
incident, and the function's existing documented fallback for a NULL
result (download-and-inspect instead) already degrades gracefully.

recent_commits.message: Fix max_files_per_repo undercounting a repo from a filtered file subset
recent_commits.body:
download_repo_files()'s file-count gate counted length(idx) -- the rows of
its OWN `files` argument for a repo -- but every caller passes a FILTERED
subset (only rows still needing a download), not the repo's true total row
count. A repo whose still-needed subset happens to fall under the cap slips
through even when its real size vastly exceeds it.

Confirmed live 2026-09-09: the exact SAPFLUXNET Zenodo record
(10.5281/zenodo.3971689, ~4000 files) this cap was built for slipped
through again on a fresh run. Several hundred individual files were then
requested from Zenodo, which was at the time answering every one with a
persistent (not transient) HTTP 403 -- confirmed directly via curl. Each
file's download retried independently and gave up, but with several hundred
files doing this one after another, the corpus run stalled on this single
paper for 4.5+ hours (7,745 "Waiting Ns for retry backoff" lines logged)
with no single wait long enough to look like the actual problem.

download_repo_files() gains repo_file_counts: an optional named vector,
repo_url -> TRUE total row count in the caller's FULL (unfiltered) listing.
When a repo is present in this vector, the gate uses it instead of
length(idx); when absent (including the default NULL), falls back to the
old length(idx) behaviour unchanged, so this is backward compatible for
any caller not yet updated.

Wired at all 9 real call sites (grepped the whole package to confirm this
is exhaustive, not just the one that caused this incident):
data_check.R's main call, code_check.R's main call (inst/modules/), and
all 7 in R/code_check.R -- .code_predownload() (the unified pre-download
step every other path defers to when code_check() runs normally) and the
four .code_expand_*() helpers (spv/smcl/mplus/html), which did not even
receive max_files_per_repo as a parameter before this (gaining it now, in
addition to repo_file_counts), plus .code_version_pin_check()'s renv.lock
and sessionInfo/README lookups. Each computes repo_file_counts from
whatever FULL listing is already in its own scope (all_files/
checked_files) before filtering to the "still needs downloading" subset
passed into download_repo_files() itself.

Also fixes a self-inflicted doc bug from an earlier commit today: R/llm.R's
new .LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS constant, inserted directly above
llm_model_list(), had absorbed that function's entire roxygen block
(title/@param/@returns/@examples) onto itself instead -- confirmed via
devtools::document() reporting "Deleting 'llm_model_list.Rd'" and writing
a stray 'dot-LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS.Rd' in its place. Moved the constant's
plain-comment block above llm_model_list()'s roxygen block instead of
between it and the function, restoring llm_model_list.Rd correctly.

recent_commits.message: Flag install.packages() calls in code_check (#398)
recent_commits.body:
code_install_packages() mirrors code_setwd()'s exact shape: scans
comment-stripped R code for install.packages(...) calls (base or
utils::-qualified), skips a match found inside a string literal
(instructional text, e.g. a message() telling the user to run it
themselves) via the same .code_pos_in_string() check code_setwd() already
uses, and returns one row per live call with its line number.

Only ever sees a LIVE call, by construction: like code_setwd(), it is
only ever called on code_remove_comments()'s output, so a commented-out
`#install.packages(...)` is invisible to it -- verified live: comment-
stripping "#install.packages('ggplot2')\nlibrary(ggplot2)" leaves only the
library() call, and code_install_packages() correctly finds nothing.

An install.packages() call in analysis code installs software on whoever
runs it without asking -- at minimum disruptive (unexpected install,
network access, an untested package version), at worst a security risk if
it points at an untrusted repository. Wired into inst/modules/code_check.R
identically to setwd() at every touch point: per-file count + call text,
the zero-column fallback's analysis_cols list, a report section + summary
table + traffic-light contribution (an install.packages() call anywhere
now blocks green, same as setwd()), and the per-paper summary_table's
code_install_packages column.

Deliberately narrower than the issue's own proposed 3-tier traffic light
(green/yellow for commented-out/red for live): confirmed with the
maintainer that only a live call should ever fire the check at all, not a
separate yellow tier for commented-out instances -- which the
comment-stripped-input design already guarantees for free.

recent_commits.message: Switch llm_model_list() from a blocklist to an allowlist of providers
recent_commits.body:
The previous fix (excluding models_posit specifically, see the earlier
commit on this same function) broke again within the same ellmer version
bump: ellmer 0.5.0 added models_update_prices() -- a maintenance utility
that refreshes cached pricing data and returns a plain logical, not a
models data frame -- which still matches the "models_.+" export pattern
llm_model_list() used to discover providers. Its boolean result reached
m$platform <- p, got coerced to a list, and crashed dplyr::bind_rows()
with "Argument 2 must be a data frame or a named atomic vector" for every
provider's results, not just this one. ellmer 0.5.0 also made
models_github() defunct (GitHub Models was retired 2026-07-30).

Confirmed live 2026-09-09 (still investigating GitHub issue #397): a fresh
install pulling ellmer 0.5.0 hit this immediately when calling
llm_model_list() (report_app()'s Options tab calls it on startup) -- the
Posit device-code login from before is gone, but the function still fails
outright, just from a different proximate cause. Patching each new
offender as it's discovered (posit, now update_prices) will keep breaking
on the next ellmer release that adds anything else matching "models_.+".

Replaced the dynamic "everything ellmer exports" discovery with an
explicit allowlist (.LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS) of the providers metacheck
actually reviews and documents supporting, intersected against whatever
the installed ellmer version exports. A genuinely new provider ellmer adds
in the future is simply not queried until someone deliberately reviews it
and adds it here, rather than being auto-adopted the moment it exists.
Also added a defensive is.data.frame(m) check before m$platform <- p, as a
second layer: even a future allowlisted provider that changes its return
shape now fails safely (skipped) instead of crashing every other
provider's results too.

Verified against a real ellmer 0.5.0 install (a fresh, isolated
pak::pkg_install of this exact commit): llm_model_list() completes in 5.4s
with no error, posit/update_prices/github all correctly absent from
results.

recent_commits.message: Exclude Posit's hosted-model gateway from llm_model_list()
recent_commits.body:
llm_model_list() dynamically calls every ellmer::models_* export to build
the model-choice list, rather than an explicit provider allowlist. A newer
ellmer release added models_posit(), which authenticates against Posit's
own hosted-model gateway (gateway.posit.ai) via an interactive OAuth
device-code browser login when no credentials are cached.

Confirmed live (GitHub issue #397): a user on a completely clean install
hit this the moment report_app() rendered its model-choice dropdown (which
calls llm_model_list() on startup, before the user does anything) -- shown
a device code and a Posit sign-in page with no relation to anything they
configured, and ended up enrolled in a "Posit AI" trial trying to make it
go away. Traced to ellmer::models_posit()'s source directly: base_url =
"https://gateway.posit.ai", credentials from default_posit_credentials().

Posit's hosted models are not a provider metacheck documents supporting,
so excluded outright (funcs$posit <- NULL) rather than credential-gated
like google_gemini/google_vertex just below (an existing guard for the
same class of bug, hit before for Google specifically).

recent_commits.message: Add FSD (Finnish Social Science Data Archive) listing support
recent_commits.body:
fsd_links()/fsd_info() mirror archive-psycharchives.R's shape: list a
study's metadata and file inventory via an open, unauthenticated API,
without downloading anything. Confirmed live 2026-09-09 against a real
study (FSD2653, "Finnish National Election Study 2011"): FSD exposes an
open DDI-C 2.5 XML metadata record per study at
services.fsd.tuni.fi/catalogue/<ID>/DDI/<ID>_eng.xml, no auth needed,
including study title, DOI, an access-restriction statement, and one
fileDscr block per data file (name, format, case/variable counts).

Unlike Dryad/Zenodo/OSF/PsychArchives, that record has NO file-level
download URI anywhere -- downloading FSD data itself requires Haka
(Finnish higher-education federated login), an Aila account, or a
per-dataset access-application form for most studies, none of which a
script can automate. So there is no fsd_file_download(): every listed file
carries file_url = NA, the same "found but inaccessible" treatment
repo_check already gives a private OSF node or a restricted PsychArchives
item. This is a genuine capability gap in FSD's own API, not an oversight
here (verified: doi.org/10.60686/t-fsd2653's DDI record was fetched and
inspected directly).

fsd_links() matches three real citation forms (catalogue URL, 10.60686 DOI,
urn.fi URN) plus a bare "FSD####" in-text mention; .fsd_study_id() extracts
a canonical study id from any of them, verified against all three live.

Not yet wired into repo_check.R's dispatch -- that integration (repo_type
detection, files_df/meta_df construction, reporting these as gated/
inaccessible like other restricted sources) is a separate follow-up.

recent_commits.message: Apply max_file_size/max_download_size caps to archive-member downloads
recent_commits.body:
An archive-member row (repo_check's zip-peek expansion: an entry found
INSIDE a .zip via byte-range listing, with no file_url of its own, fetched
through .zip_fetch_members()'s per-member range-request mechanism instead)
was invisible to both size caps entirely. The archive-member block runs
before, and independently of, the per-repo budget loop that enforces
max_file_size/max_download_size for ordinary file_url downloads, and the
code said as much ("Does not touch a row with a real file_url, so this is
purely additive for archive-member rows") without applying any cap of its
own.

Confirmed live 2026-09-09 against a real OSF repository (Cooper corpus,
paper 10_1111_1365_2435_14173) whose zip-peek listing named several 1-2 GB
CSV members: every one downloaded in full, 8.1 GB total for one paper,
despite max_file_size = 100 (MB) and max_download_size = 500 (MB) both set.
data_check then read each multi-GB file in full and classified every
column, taking ~42 minutes for that single paper.

Now applies the same per-file cap (an oversize member is skipped, recorded
in oversize_skipped for the existing reporting) and a per-ARCHIVE budget
(smallest members first, up to the cap) before fetching. Scoped per archive
rather than per repository -- unifying budgets across the archive-member and
file_url paths would need the two paths merged, which this does not
attempt; this closes the specific gap that let one archive's members bypass
sizing entirely. Verified the filtering arithmetic in isolation against
this paper's real member sizes: 8 of 15 members excluded by the per-file
cap, the remaining 7 fit the 500 MB budget at 312.6 MB used (was 8.1 GB).

recent_commits.message: Silence knitr::purl()'s harmless per-chunk stderr spam in code_extract_r()
recent_commits.body:
A chunk HEADER that references a variable only ever defined by an earlier
CODE chunk (e.g. a chunk option like fig.width=x, set by a preceding chunk)
fails to evaluate under purl()/tangle mode, since tangle mode extracts code
without ever running it. Confirmed live against a real repository in the
Cooper corpus (Zenodo 4721453, OHI-Northeast, documents/methods/
layers_all.Rmd): this one file printed 23 lines of "Error in eval(x, envir
= envir) : object 'x' not found" during a corpus-validation run, yet
knitr::purl() still returned the complete, correctly extracted code (144
lines). This is knitr's own internal per-chunk recovery -- it writes the
caught error straight to the stderr connection (not an R condition; neither
tryCatch(error = ...) nor a message() handler catches it) rather than
raising anything, so one broken chunk header does not abort the rest of the
document. The lines are therefore not a real failure, but they read exactly
like a crash in a long-running corpus log, and a document with many
dynamically-optioned chunks can print this many times over. Redirected via
sink(type = "message") instead, since that is the only thing that catches
output bypassing R's condition system entirely.

Also fixes an incidental bug found in the same function: its two on.exit()
calls lacked add = TRUE, so the second silently replaced the first and the
temp output file was never actually deleted on a normal call (only the
knitr option reset ran).

recent_commits.message: Fix data_check crash and wasted work in date/datetime column classification
recent_commits.body:
strptime() (via as.POSIXct's format parser) hard-errors -- rather than
returning NA -- on an input string longer than ~1000 characters (confirmed
live: R's internal strptime buffer is fixed-size). A free-text column (e.g.
an open-ended survey response) routinely has values that long, and
.parse_frac() crashed the entire data_check module the moment such a column
reached it, not just that one column. Confirmed as the exact cause of three
separate corpus-rerun crashes on the same paper (2026-09-03, 2026-09-05,
2026-09-08). Overlong values are now treated as unparseable (NA) instead.

Separately, .parse_frac() is also called for any column whose NAME suggests
a date (e.g. a column literally named "day"), regardless of whether the
column's VALUES are already known to be numeric. A strptime-style format can
never match a bare number, so this always returned 0, just slowly: up to 18
as.POSIXct() passes over the full column. Measured live on a real 331k-row
Darwin Core dataset from the corpus: a numeric "day" column alone cost 2.27s
of an 11.3s total classification pass (~10x every other column). Skipping
straight to 0 for a numeric column changes no result, only the time to
reach it -- confirmed the same file now classifies in 8.9s, with "day" at
0.02s.

recent_commits.message: Add optional on-disk cache for repo_check's own listing/API calls
recent_commits.body:
repo_check() gains cache = TRUE (off by default), threaded through every
host it queries with a real API call: Dryad, Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare,
ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, OSF, GitHub, GitLab, and PsychArchives. Each
repository's listing result (what files it has) is now cached separately
from the downloaded file bytes (which repo_cache_dir() already caches).

Root cause: a restart re-issues every listing call from scratch even for a
repository whose files are already fully downloaded. During the Cooper
corpus rerun, 11 restarts x 40+ Dryad listing calls each (2 requests per
dataset) produced 440+ redundant requests against a workload that genuinely
needed a handful -- this repeated re-listing, not the actual download
volume, was what exhausted Dryad's rate limit. Caching the listing makes a
restart free for anything already listed once.

A transient failure (host down, 404, parse error) is never cached -- only a
successfully-listed result is written, via .repo_info_ok()/
.repo_info_list_ok(), so a later restart still retries a genuine miss rather
than replaying a cached failure forever. ResearchBox needed no change: it
has no listing API (listing IS the download), and already reuses a
previously-downloaded archive unconditionally via the existing file-bytes
cache.

recent_commits.message: Fix zip download streaming to actually respect its own timeout
recent_commits.body:
.download_zip_to_cache()'s deadline check (Sys.time() > deadline) only
ran BETWEEN calls to httr2::resp_stream_raw(), never during one -- a
single stalled read defeated the timeout entirely, since
req_perform_connection()'s default blocking=TRUE mode makes that read
block indefinitely rather than returning control to the loop.

Confirmed live: a real ~65MB OSF Waterbutler zip download (326-file
repository, osf.io/wdzay) stalled mid-stream for 45+ minutes with the
underlying TCP connection sitting in CLOSE_WAIT (the remote had already
closed its side), consuming real CPU and growing memory the whole time,
with zero indication anything was wrong until the process was killed and
inspected directly.

Fixed by opening the connection with blocking=FALSE, so a zero-length
read genuinely means "no data yet" rather than blocking, and adding a
short Sys.sleep() on that branch so the loop still returns control to the
deadline check every iteration without busy-looping the CPU.

Also scales the timeout itself against the transfer's own expected size
(the sum of the selected files' sizes, already computed by every call
site to decide zip-vs-file-by-file) at a conservative 200KB/s floor,
extracted as its own testable .zip_timeout_for_size() helper -- a fixed
timeout is either too short for a large, honestly slow archive or too
long for a small stalled one to fail fast.

recent_commits.body:
Confirmed against real corpus files (data_availability validation): a
paper whose only listed files were sequencing data in FASTA/FASTQ
format (e.g. "76_SE_0.01.fasta.gz", "thal_MK380719_TGCA.1.fq.gz") had
every one of those files fall through to "unknown", since neither
.ext_registry (data_classify_files()'s format lock) nor
metacheck::file_types (file_category()'s own lookup table) knew these
extensions -- wrongly reading such a paper as having no data available
at all, when real research data was genuinely present.

Adds the bare extensions (fasta/fa/fq/fastq) to .ext_registry and their
gzip-compressed forms (fasta.gz/fa.gz/fq.gz/fastq.gz -- the common
convention for these, since sequence files compress well) to
file_types, both as data_type "data". The compressed forms also
required a new file_category() compound-type rule (ft_has("data") &
ft_has("archive")): a name like "sample.fasta.gz" matches both its own
compound data extension and the bare "gz" extension (typed "archive"),
so its filetype comes out "data;archive" -- previously fell through to
NA for any such compound, an existing latent gap this specific,
newly-possible compound now exposed. ".dat" and a bare ".info" stay
deliberately unlocked (too generic on their own to safely classify),

recent_commits.message: Fix silent truncation of zip members over 32KB (#384)
recent_commits.body:
.zip_inflate_member() called zip::inflate() with size = NULL, because
passing the member's known uncompressed size raised "Failed to inflate
data" (an apparent quirk of the zip package's exact-size path). Leaving
size unset avoids that error, but its documented "resize the output
buffer multiple times" behaviour does not happen in practice: any
member larger than the default 32768-byte buffer came back silently
truncated at exactly 32768 bytes, with no error or warning.

and discarded the bytes, so this looked identical to a genuine network
or host-compatibility failure -- accounting for the large majority of
issue #384's code_download disagreements in the Cooper et al.
validation (confirmed live against real Zenodo-hosted zip members).

modes and was verified against real Zenodo members both under and over
32KB, plus a new offline regression test using a local zip.

expansion always intended (see its own prior comment) so a discovered

(see #384).

(20/hour -- separate from, and much tighter than, the 100/day ceiling)
was still being tripped repeatedly. Confirmed live against the real

zip request on three consecutive restarts, because restarting the
script does not reset the host's quota clock -- only real elapsed time
does, and not enough had passed between attempts.

datasets): threshold 4 needs 190 zip requests corpus-wide, a 9.5/hour
average even under the best-case 2-day spread -- already exceeding the
20/hour ceiling on average, before accounting for a real run's uneven,
bursty pacing. Threshold 12 needs only 33 zip requests corpus-wide
(1.6/hour average), a far larger safety margin against the hourly wall
specifically.

This trades away some of the daily-quota-optimality the original
threshold-sweep found (12 is not that sweep's minimum-day threshold,
3-6 was) for practical hourly headroom that matters more once a real
run is actually hitting the hourly cap repeatedly.

clean (FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 1 | PASS 77).

recent_commits.message: Make Dryad's zip-vs-file-by-file download choice quota-aware
recent_commits.body:
Dryad throttles zip downloads and per-file downloads through two
independent per-IP quota buckets with very different sizes (confirmed
2026-09-01 against Dryad's own open-source rate-limit config,
datadryad/dryad-app config/initializers/rack_attack.rb +
config/app_config.yml): zip_downloads_per_day = 100,
file_downloads_per_day = 500 -- 5x more headroom on the file bucket.

The existing zip-vs-file decision only weighed request-count efficiency
(worth_it <- n_wanted > 50 || record_n <= 2*n_wanted), which picks zip
for nearly every real dataset since callers almost always want "all of
it". That means every Dryad dataset routed through the strict 100/day
zip bucket while the much larger 500/day file bucket sat unused.

Recomputed against the real Cooper-validation corpus (768 Dryad
datasets, 2710 files, 26 completed batches): always-zip needs 8
calendar days minimum (768 requests / 100 per day); always-file needs
6 (2710 / 500); routing small datasets (<=4 files) to the file bucket
and only larger ones to the zip bucket needs 3 -- the minimum across
every threshold from 0-50 tested, because it's the point where both
buckets fill up on the same day instead of one sitting idle while the
other alone is the bottleneck.

Added a `quota_worth_it <- n_wanted > 4L` gate ANDed onto the existing
request-count check, Dryad-only. Not applied to OSF/Zenodo/Dataverse/
GitHub/GitLab's identical-looking worth_it lines elsewhere in the same
file -- only Dryad's independent-stacked-throttle asymmetry has been
confirmed; changing the shared logic for hosts whose rate-limit
behaviour was never verified would be a separate, unjustified change.

Two new unit tests confirm a small Dryad dataset skips zip even though
the old request-count-only logic would have picked it, and a larger
one still uses zip. Full package test suite passes clean
(FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 68 | PASS 4327).

recent_commits.message: Wait for the real rate-limit reset instead of blind exponential backoff
recent_commits.body:
Found while investigating a code_check crash in a real 1861-paper corpus
run: Dryad's file-download endpoint sends IETF-draft RateLimit-Limit/
RateLimit-Remaining/RateLimit-Reset headers on a 429 -- confirmed live,
the limit is 100 requests/hour, reset on a fixed clock-hour boundary, and
NOT raised by OAuth authentication (despite this session's earlier
dryad_auth() work assuming it would be). The existing .storage_backoff()
only recognises the older Retry-After header, which Dryad never sends at
all, so every retry did blind exponential backoff (2s/4s/8s.../30s cap)
against a bucket that was provably empty until the next hour -- repeatedly
re-triggering the same wasted retry storm for every file in every affected
dataset, and very likely a major contributing factor to the heavy-429
conditions that preceded the crash.

The same header family (or the older X-RateLimit-* convention) is
confirmed live on Zenodo, GitHub, and GitLab too -- all four backends this
session has touched -- so this is built as shared logic across every
download call site, not a Dryad-specific patch. OSF/Figshare/Dataverse do
not expose it on the endpoints checked and are unaffected either way.

- .rate_limit_wait(): reads either header family off a 429 response,
  returns the real wait in seconds or NA if unconfirmed/absent.
- .storage_retry_after_factory() / .storage_is_transient_factory(): wired
  into req_retry()'s after/is_transient at every per-file download call
  site (.download_one(), .download_many_parallel()), so a
  confirmed-exhausted 429 waits for the REAL reset instead of blind
  backoff.
- .download_zip_to_cache() (the whole-dataset zip path) gains its own
  rate-limit check too: previously a 429's small error-page body would
  reach the streaming loop and either fail unzip() with a confusing
  "not a zip file" error or (worse) get silently treated as if it were
  real archive bytes. Now checks the status explicitly and waits for a
  confirmed reset (one retry) before falling through to the caller's
  file-by-file fallback.
- req_retry()'s own waits are completely silent by default -- a
  multi-minute-to-hour-long wait with zero console output looks identical
  to a hung process. A message() now announces any wait over 5 seconds,
  with the exact duration and how to skip it.
- New skip_on_api_limit parameter on download_repo_files() (default
  FALSE, i.e. always wait for the real reset -- explicit decision: the
  goal is completeness, not speed, for an unattended corpus build). TRUE
  gives up on a confirmed-exhausted request immediately instead, recorded
  in the failed attribute with an "API rate limit exhausted: "-prefixed
  message, filterable from every other kind of failure, so a caller can
  retry those specific files later once the quota has reset.

8 new unit tests in test-repo-download.R (1 skipped: an httr2
local_mocked_responses()/req_retry() interaction confirmed to behave
unreliably specifically under full-suite test ordering, not a bug in the
fix -- covered instead by an adjacent test using the more reliable
local_mocked_bindings() mock path; see that test's own comment). Full
package suite otherwise unaffected: FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 68 | PASS 4314.

_new_commits.message: Cache zip_peek() failures too, not just successes
_new_commits.body:
zip_peek()'s per-session cache only ever remembered a SUCCESS; a NULL
(host refused, rate-limited, or otherwise) was deliberately retried fresh
on every call, on the documented assumption that "a real 'not supported'
result would still return NULL again quickly."

That assumption holds for a host that plainly does not honour range
requests (a fast, clear refusal), but confirmed live 2026-09-09 to be false
when the host instead answers every call with a retryable-looking status
(403/429/5xx) persistently: a single zip_peek() call already pays
req_retry()'s full backoff sequence (up to 3 tries each, exponential up to
a 30s cap, across up to 3 separate HTTP calls this function and its
helpers make) before giving up. This file's own header comment already
documents that the SAME url is peeked more than once per pipeline run
(once in repo_check, again in download_repo_files()'s
.zip_fetch_members()) -- each call independently paying that cost again is
exactly what compounded a single persistently-403ing Zenodo archive
(SAPFLUXNET, 10.5281/zenodo.3971689, investigated the same day) into a
multi-hour stall, alongside the separate max_files_per_repo undercounting
bug fixed just before this.

Now caches a NULL result too (exists(url, envir=..., inherits=FALSE), not
mget's ifnotfound, so a cached failure is distinguishable from "never
attempted" -- confirmed live that assign(url, NULL, envir=...) really does
bind NULL in an environment, unlike env$x <- NULL on a list, which removes
the element). Trade-off: a transient failure that would have cleared by a
LATER call in the same session is no longer retried fresh either -- judged
acceptable, since the alternative (repeating a costly multi-minute retry
sequence every time the same URL is touched again) is what caused this
incident, and the function's existing documented fallback for a NULL
result (download-and-inspect instead) already degrades gracefully.

_new_commits.message: Fix max_files_per_repo undercounting a repo from a filtered file subset
_new_commits.body:
download_repo_files()'s file-count gate counted length(idx) -- the rows of
its OWN `files` argument for a repo -- but every caller passes a FILTERED
subset (only rows still needing a download), not the repo's true total row
count. A repo whose still-needed subset happens to fall under the cap slips
through even when its real size vastly exceeds it.

Confirmed live 2026-09-09: the exact SAPFLUXNET Zenodo record
(10.5281/zenodo.3971689, ~4000 files) this cap was built for slipped
through again on a fresh run. Several hundred individual files were then
requested from Zenodo, which was at the time answering every one with a
persistent (not transient) HTTP 403 -- confirmed directly via curl. Each
file's download retried independently and gave up, but with several hundred
files doing this one after another, the corpus run stalled on this single
paper for 4.5+ hours (7,745 "Waiting Ns for retry backoff" lines logged)
with no single wait long enough to look like the actual problem.

download_repo_files() gains repo_file_counts: an optional named vector,
repo_url -> TRUE total row count in the caller's FULL (unfiltered) listing.
When a repo is present in this vector, the gate uses it instead of
length(idx); when absent (including the default NULL), falls back to the
old length(idx) behaviour unchanged, so this is backward compatible for
any caller not yet updated.

Wired at all 9 real call sites (grepped the whole package to confirm this
is exhaustive, not just the one that caused this incident):
data_check.R's main call, code_check.R's main call (inst/modules/), and
all 7 in R/code_check.R -- .code_predownload() (the unified pre-download
step every other path defers to when code_check() runs normally) and the
four .code_expand_*() helpers (spv/smcl/mplus/html), which did not even
receive max_files_per_repo as a parameter before this (gaining it now, in
addition to repo_file_counts), plus .code_version_pin_check()'s renv.lock
and sessionInfo/README lookups. Each computes repo_file_counts from
whatever FULL listing is already in its own scope (all_files/
checked_files) before filtering to the "still needs downloading" subset
passed into download_repo_files() itself.

Also fixes a self-inflicted doc bug from an earlier commit today: R/llm.R's
new .LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS constant, inserted directly above
llm_model_list(), had absorbed that function's entire roxygen block
(title/@param/@returns/@examples) onto itself instead -- confirmed via

a stray 'dot-LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS.Rd' in its place. Moved the constant's
plain-comment block above llm_model_list()'s roxygen block instead of
between it and the function, restoring llm_model_list.Rd correctly.

code_install_packages() mirrors code_setwd()'s exact shape: scans
comment-stripped R code for install.packages(...) calls (base or

(instructional text, e.g. a message() telling the user to run it

it points at an untrusted repository. Wired into inst/modules/code_check.R
identically to setwd() at every touch point: per-file count + call text,

_new_commits.body:
The previous fix (excluding models_posit specifically, see the earlier
commit on this same function) broke again within the same ellmer version
bump: ellmer 0.5.0 added models_update_prices() -- a maintenance utility
that refreshes cached pricing data and returns a plain logical, not a
models data frame -- which still matches the "models_.+" export pattern
llm_model_list() used to discover providers. Its boolean result reached
m$platform <- p, got coerced to a list, and crashed dplyr::bind_rows()
with "Argument 2 must be a data frame or a named atomic vector" for every
provider's results, not just this one. ellmer 0.5.0 also made
models_github() defunct (GitHub Models was retired 2026-07-30).

Confirmed live 2026-09-09 (still investigating GitHub issue #397): a fresh
install pulling ellmer 0.5.0 hit this immediately when calling
llm_model_list() (report_app()'s Options tab calls it on startup) -- the
Posit device-code login from before is gone, but the function still fails
outright, just from a different proximate cause. Patching each new
offender as it's discovered (posit, now update_prices) will keep breaking
on the next ellmer release that adds anything else matching "models_.+".

Replaced the dynamic "everything ellmer exports" discovery with an
explicit allowlist (.LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS) of the providers metacheck
actually reviews and documents supporting, intersected against whatever
the installed ellmer version exports. A genuinely new provider ellmer adds
in the future is simply not queried until someone deliberately reviews it
and adds it here, rather than being auto-adopted the moment it exists.
Also added a defensive is.data.frame(m) check before m$platform <- p, as a
second layer: even a future allowlisted provider that changes its return
shape now fails safely (skipped) instead of crashing every other
provider's results too.

pak::pkg_install of this exact commit): llm_model_list() completes in 5.4s
with no error, posit/update_prices/github all correctly absent from
results.

_new_commits.message: Add FSD (Finnish Social Science Data Archive) listing support
_new_commits.body:
fsd_links()/fsd_info() mirror archive-psycharchives.R's shape: list a
study's metadata and file inventory via an open, unauthenticated API,
without downloading anything. Confirmed live 2026-09-09 against a real
study (FSD2653, "Finnish National Election Study 2011"): FSD exposes an
open DDI-C 2.5 XML metadata record per study at
services.fsd.tuni.fi/catalogue/<ID>/DDI/<ID>_eng.xml, no auth needed,
including study title, DOI, an access-restriction statement, and one
fileDscr block per data file (name, format, case/variable counts).

Unlike Dryad/Zenodo/OSF/PsychArchives, that record has NO file-level
download URI anywhere -- downloading FSD data itself requires Haka
(Finnish higher-education federated login), an Aila account, or a
per-dataset access-application form for most studies, none of which a
script can automate. So there is no fsd_file_download(): every listed file
carries file_url = NA, the same "found but inaccessible" treatment
repo_check already gives a private OSF node or a restricted PsychArchives
item. This is a genuine capability gap in FSD's own API, not an oversight
here (verified: doi.org/10.60686/t-fsd2653's DDI record was fetched and
inspected directly).

fsd_links() matches three real citation forms (catalogue URL, 10.60686 DOI,
urn.fi URN) plus a bare "FSD####" in-text mention; .fsd_study_id() extracts
a canonical study id from any of them, verified against all three live.

Not yet wired into repo_check.R's dispatch -- that integration (repo_type
detection, files_df/meta_df construction, reporting these as gated/
inaccessible like other restricted sources) is a separate follow-up.

_new_commits.message: Apply max_file_size/max_download_size caps to archive-member downloads
_new_commits.body:
An archive-member row (repo_check's zip-peek expansion: an entry found
INSIDE a .zip via byte-range listing, with no file_url of its own, fetched
through .zip_fetch_members()'s per-member range-request mechanism instead)
was invisible to both size caps entirely. The archive-member block runs
before, and independently of, the per-repo budget loop that enforces
max_file_size/max_download_size for ordinary file_url downloads, and the
code said as much ("Does not touch a row with a real file_url, so this is
purely additive for archive-member rows") without applying any cap of its
own.

Confirmed live 2026-09-09 against a real OSF repository (Cooper corpus,
paper 10_1111_1365_2435_14173) whose zip-peek listing named several 1-2 GB
CSV members: every one downloaded in full, 8.1 GB total for one paper,
despite max_file_size = 100 (MB) and max_download_size = 500 (MB) both set.
data_check then read each multi-GB file in full and classified every
column, taking ~42 minutes for that single paper.

Now applies the same per-file cap (an oversize member is skipped, recorded
in oversize_skipped for the existing reporting) and a per-ARCHIVE budget
(smallest members first, up to the cap) before fetching. Scoped per archive
rather than per repository -- unifying budgets across the archive-member and
file_url paths would need the two paths merged, which this does not
attempt; this closes the specific gap that let one archive's members bypass
sizing entirely. Verified the filtering arithmetic in isolation against
this paper's real member sizes: 8 of 15 members excluded by the per-file
cap, the remaining 7 fit the 500 MB budget at 312.6 MB used (was 8.1 GB).

recent_commits.message: docs(changelog): drop the absolute offsets — they do not transfer; keep the gap, which does
recent_commits.body:
843394a published `char 60080 intact / char 60155 destroyed` from a consumer's pre-fix store.
The labels were right, but the numbers should not have been published at all, and measuring it
here is what showed why:

    consumer's 1.9.57 store   HapMap3 @ 60080   HapMap * @ 60155
    my 1.9.65 re-extraction   HapMap3 @ 60110   HapMap3   @ 60185

SAME PAPER, SAME TWO OCCURRENCES, DIFFERENT ABSOLUTE POSITIONS. An offset is a property of one
extraction's exact text, not of the defect, so a consumer running `grep -ob` against its own
store would meet a discrepancy with an entirely mundane cause -- while already anxious about
corrupted data. Byte and character offsets differ AGAIN within a single file (43 bytes of
multi-byte UTF-8 upstream in that store, so `grep -ob` reports 60096 where python reports
60080), which would force the unit to be stated as well.

WHAT TRANSFERS IS THE GAP, and it is the load-bearing half: the two occurrences are 75 apart,
IDENTICAL IN CHARACTERS AND IN BYTES, measured independently by both parties on two different
extractions. The text between them is a single sentence boundary:

    HapMap3 SNPs. Inclusion in the LD Score regression analysis was limited to

So "same token, same paragraph, 75 apart, one rewritten and one not" survives every way of
measuring it, and that is the sentence a consumer needs. The counts (`HapMap3` = 1,
`HapMap *` = 1 pre-fix) are the other durable part. The offsets were the most fragile thing in
the block and the only part nobody could reproduce.

The general point, worth more than this edit: A NUMBER THAT CANNOT BE REPRODUCED BY THE AUDIENCE
IS NOT EVIDENCE TO THEM, IT IS AN INVITATION TO A CONTRADICTION. Publish the invariant, not the
coordinate.

Raised by the consumer that supplied the original figures, who also corrected their own prose
(they had described character offsets as byte offsets). Verified here rather than relayed.

recent_commits.message: docs(changelog): the pre-fix half — 2 in the source, 1 destroyed, 75 characters apart
recent_commits.body:
5036c9a reproduced the POST-fix side from the custody PDF (HapMap3 = 2 at normalization 1.9.65)
and that settled whether the original claim held. It could not show what an AFFECTED file looks
like, because docpluck no longer produces one. The consumer supplied that half from its own
1.9.57 store, with byte offsets and a control this time:

    corpus-text__docpluck-norm@1.9.57.txt  (112,876 B)
      char 60080  INTACT     "...focusing on HapMap3 SNPs. Inclusion in the LD Score regression..."
      char 60155  DESTROYED  "...limited to HapMap * SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF)..."
      HapMap3 = 1     HapMap * = 1     HapMap 3 = 0

Put beside the post-fix measurement the whole picture is there: 2 occurrences in the source, 1
destroyed before the fix, 0 after.

THE TWO SURVIVORS ARE 75 CHARACTERS APART, IN CONSECUTIVE SENTENCES. That is the sharpest
statement of why a single site settles nothing: the same token, the same paragraph, one rewritten
and one not. A scan that stops at the first hit reads whichever it happens to meet, and either
answer is defensible from the evidence it looked at.

ONE PRACTICAL SOFTENING, and it is the consumer's correction to my wording rather than mine: an
intact sibling may sit nearby, so a consumer can SOMETIMES recover the original by scanning.
Re-extraction at 1.9.65+ is the RELIABLE route, not the ONLY one. An intermediate revision of the
notice said "only", which overstates the damage and would send someone re-running a pipeline when
a grep would have answered it.

For the record on the exchange that produced this: their retraction and my re-correction crossed
in flight, so their "STOP, revert 0febe36" arrived after 5036c9a had already reverted it. Both
sides converged on the same reproduced answer independently, which is the useful property of
having measured it rather than argued it.

recent_commits.message: docs(changelog): withdraw yesterday's correction — I published a consumer's claim without reproducing it
recent_commits.body:
The paragraph added in 0febe36 said "both forms coexist" is not a general property of the W0k
damage, on a consumer's report that its copy of 10.1038/s41562-024-02076-3 held only the
destroyed form. Its author has withdrawn it. **The error on this side is that I edited a PUBLIC
document on a relayed measurement I had not reproduced** -- and this project's own rule is that a
reviewer's finding is a HYPOTHESIS until a local reproduction confirms it. Two hops, no
verification, and it reached the public CHANGELOG and the notice every consumer is acting on.

REPRODUCED NOW, at the source, which is what should have happened first:

    10.1038/s41562-024-02076-3, re-extracted from the custody PDF at normalization 1.9.65
      HapMap3  = 2       HapMap 3 = 0       HapMap * = 0
        "...focusing on HapMap3 SNPs. Inclusion in the LD Score regression..."
        "...analysis was limited to HapMap3 SNPs with a minor allele frequency..."

    10.1073/pnas.2313604121, same method
      Deposited 3 = 1    Deposited * = 0
        "Deposited 3 December 2022."

Both occurrences of the identifier are `HapMap3` in the source, and the pre-fix pipeline
destroyed exactly ONE of the two. So the ORIGINAL claim was right and is now measured rather than
relayed, and the date shape is independently confirmed rather than taken on trust.

THE RULE RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, and only one half was written down before: a single clean site
cannot clear a document, AND a single destroyed site does not condemn one. Count every
occurrence.

HOW THE WRONG CLAIM WAS MANUFACTURED, because the mechanism is more useful than the correction.
The consumer verified with `grep -c 'HapMap 3'` -- WITH A SPACE -- against an intact form that
has none. They searched for a string that cannot exist, got 0, and read that zero as a finding.
`HapMap 3` returns 0 against a fully intact file; the trap is now demonstrated rather than
predicted, and it fired in the SAME message that flagged the no-space trap to others.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE LESSON. Their 30-file statistics scan carried two-sided controls and held up
completely. The claim that failed was a one-line verification grep, where nobody thinks to plant
a control. Knowing a failure mode by name does not prevent it; a control does, and effort tracks
the ceremony of the check rather than the weight of the conclusion drawn from it.

Nothing else in 0febe36 is affected: the date shape stands (verified above), and the measured
"no published statistic corrupted across 30 files" result stands with its controls intact.

recent_commits.message: docs(changelog): "both forms coexist" is NOT general, and W0k also destroyed a bare DATE digit
recent_commits.body:
Two corrections to the 2.4.140 section, both from a consumer's own measurement rather than from
this repo, and both making the picture WORSE in one direction and better in another.

1. THE RECOVERY CLAIM WAS TOO OPTIMISTIC. This file said `10.1038/s41562-024-02076-3` holds both
   `HapMap3 SNPs.` intact and `HapMap *` destroyed, and drew "a single clean site cannot clear a
   document". True of the copy examined here. But in the CONSUMER'S copy at normalization 1.9.57
   the token is destroyed at EVERY occurrence -- `HapMap3` count 0, `HapMap 3` count 0 -- so
   there is nothing in that file to recover from. "Both forms coexist" is a property of one
   extraction, not of the defect. Re-extraction from the source PDF is then the only route, which
   is a materially different instruction to give a consumer.

2. A THIRD SHAPE, WITH A REAL DOI. `10.1073/pnas.2313604121` shipped `Deposited * December 2022.`
   for `Deposited 3 December 2022.` -- a bare day-of-month digit with SPACES ON BOTH SIDES. Every
   example previously recorded (HapMap3, ASL TO3, GRCh3, Material 3, x3) was a digit glued to a
   word or an identifier, so a pattern anchored to that shape misses this class entirely. Verified
   by re-extracting the custody PDF through a service at identity 2.4.141/3f035f5/clean, not by
   pattern-matching. This meets the project's standing rule that a case comes from a real paper
   with the DOI recorded, never from a constructed string.

   Two grep traps follow and are now written down: the intact form is `HapMap3` with NO space, so
   grepping `HapMap 3` returns 0 and reads as a failed fix; and the standalone-digit class needs
   its own pattern.

3. THE REASSURING HALF, AND IT IS MEASURED. Across that consumer's 30-file corpus NO PUBLISHED
   STATISTIC was corrupted. The unambiguous signature is a star sandwiched between digits -- a
   significance star can never sit there -- and it returned 0 sites in 30 files under a TWO-SIDED
   control: planted `12*4` and `0.6*9` caught, planted `0.695***` and `0.34**` ignored, 1,094
   asterisks counted to prove the files were read, and 0 surviving `×`/`✕`/`⨯` glyphs to prove the
   asterisk surface was complete rather than a subset. The damage class is identifiers, names and
   dates -- not statistics.

THEIR PROCESS IS WORTH RECORDING AS MUCH AS THEIR RESULT. Their first scan flagged
`240 participants * 8 items` as corruption and the NEGATIVE control caught it. A later pass
reported "0 corrupted statistics" while its own POSITIVE control was dead -- the planted string
contained no genuine digit-star-digit, so the pattern had never been exercised and that zero was
untested rather than clean. Both are exactly the "a zero is a claim about the instrument" failure

recent_commits.message: directive: THE THREE TIERS -- what a rewrite must earn, and the test that decides
recent_commits.body:
User directive 2026-09-06, after W0k was found destroying real published digits in
production. Makes the existing 'EXTRACTS AND NORMALIZES, DOES NOT FIX THE PAPER' rule
mechanically applicable instead of a judgement call:

- the gate test: if every surrounding word and number were replaced with garbage, would the
  same evidence still justify the output? No -> repair -> forbidden.
- three tiers: Notation / Channel repair / File lie. The tier decides, not confidence.
- signal convergence only counts across DIFFERENT PHYSICAL ORIGINS. The declared encoding
  and the glyph names are one font dictionary wearing two hats; in the efendic case
  /Differences and /ToUnicode AGREE, and the contradiction is against the printed page.
- corollary that kills a class of proposed fixes: a rule whose signature is text: str can
  never consult the page, so it can never be licensed for a file lie.
- key every rule on an evidence class, never a font, publisher or DOI. A font is a test
  fixture, never a branch in the code.
- no rule ships or survives without its corpus firing count AND how many were correct.

Derived from a cross-model review across three independent providers.

highlights.message: Cache zip_peek() failures too, not just successes
highlights.body:
zip_peek()'s per-session cache only ever remembered a SUCCESS; a NULL
(host refused, rate-limited, or otherwise) was deliberately retried fresh
on every call, on the documented assumption that "a real 'not supported'
result would still return NULL again quickly."

That assumption holds for a host that plainly does not honour range
requests (a fast, clear refusal), but confirmed live 2026-09-09 to be false
when the host instead answers every call with a retryable-looking status
(403/429/5xx) persistently: a single zip_peek() call already pays
req_retry()'s full backoff sequence (up to 3 tries each, exponential up to
a 30s cap, across up to 3 separate HTTP calls this function and its
helpers make) before giving up. This file's own header comment already
documents that the SAME url is peeked more than once per pipeline run
(once in repo_check, again in download_repo_files()'s
.zip_fetch_members()) -- each call independently paying that cost again is
exactly what compounded a single persistently-403ing Zenodo archive
(SAPFLUXNET, 10.5281/zenodo.3971689, investigated the same day) into a
multi-hour stall, alongside the separate max_files_per_repo undercounting
bug fixed just before this.

Now caches a NULL result too (exists(url, envir=..., inherits=FALSE), not
mget's ifnotfound, so a cached failure is distinguishable from "never
attempted" -- confirmed live that assign(url, NULL, envir=...) really does
bind NULL in an environment, unlike env$x <- NULL on a list, which removes
the element). Trade-off: a transient failure that would have cleared by a
LATER call in the same session is no longer retried fresh either -- judged
acceptable, since the alternative (repeating a costly multi-minute retry
sequence every time the same URL is touched again) is what caused this
incident, and the function's existing documented fallback for a NULL

highlights.message: Fix max_files_per_repo undercounting a repo from a filtered file subset
highlights.body:
download_repo_files()'s file-count gate counted length(idx) -- the rows of
its OWN `files` argument for a repo -- but every caller passes a FILTERED
subset (only rows still needing a download), not the repo's true total row
count. A repo whose still-needed subset happens to fall under the cap slips
through even when its real size vastly exceeds it.

Confirmed live 2026-09-09: the exact SAPFLUXNET Zenodo record
(10.5281/zenodo.3971689, ~4000 files) this cap was built for slipped
through again on a fresh run. Several hundred individual files were then
requested from Zenodo, which was at the time answering every one with a
persistent (not transient) HTTP 403 -- confirmed directly via curl. Each
file's download retried independently and gave up, but with several hundred
files doing this one after another, the corpus run stalled on this single
paper for 4.5+ hours (7,745 "Waiting Ns for retry backoff" lines logged)
with no single wait long enough to look like the actual problem.

download_repo_files() gains repo_file_counts: an optional named vector,
repo_url -> TRUE total row count in the caller's FULL (unfiltered) listing.
When a repo is present in this vector, the gate uses it instead of
length(idx); when absent (including the default NULL), falls back to the
old length(idx) behaviour unchanged, so this is backward compatible for
any caller not yet updated.

Wired at all 9 real call sites (grepped the whole package to confirm this
is exhaustive, not just the one that caused this incident):
data_check.R's main call, code_check.R's main call (inst/modules/), and
all 7 in R/code_check.R -- .code_predownload() (the unified pre-download
step every other path defers to when code_check() runs normally) and the
four .code_expand_*() helpers (spv/smcl/mplus/html), which did not even
receive max_files_per_repo as a parameter before this (gaining it now, in
addition to repo_file_counts), plus .code_version_pin_check()'s renv.lock
and sessionInfo/README lookups. Each computes repo_file_counts from
whatever FULL listing is already in its own scope (all_files/
checked_files) before filtering to the "still needs downloading" subset
passed into download_repo_files() itself.

Also fixes a self-inflicted doc bug from an earlier commit today: R/llm.R's
new .LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS constant, inserted directly above
llm_model_list(), had absorbed that function's entire roxygen block
(title/@param/@returns/@examples) onto itself instead -- confirmed via
devtools::document() reporting "Deleting 'llm_model_list.Rd'" and writing
a stray 'dot-LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS.Rd' in its place. Moved the constant's
plain-comment block above llm_model_list()'s roxygen block instead of
between it and the function, restoring llm_model_list.Rd correctly.

highlights.message: Flag install.packages() calls in code_check (#398)
highlights.body:
code_install_packages() mirrors code_setwd()'s exact shape: scans
comment-stripped R code for install.packages(...) calls (base or
utils::-qualified), skips a match found inside a string literal
(instructional text, e.g. a message() telling the user to run it
themselves) via the same .code_pos_in_string() check code_setwd() already
uses, and returns one row per live call with its line number.

Only ever sees a LIVE call, by construction: like code_setwd(), it is
only ever called on code_remove_comments()'s output, so a commented-out
`#install.packages(...)` is invisible to it -- verified live: comment-
stripping "#install.packages('ggplot2')\nlibrary(ggplot2)" leaves only the
library() call, and code_install_packages() correctly finds nothing.

An install.packages() call in analysis code installs software on whoever
runs it without asking -- at minimum disruptive (unexpected install,
network access, an untested package version), at worst a security risk if
it points at an untrusted repository. Wired into inst/modules/code_check.R
identically to setwd() at every touch point: per-file count + call text,
the zero-column fallback's analysis_cols list, a report section + summary
table + traffic-light contribution (an install.packages() call anywhere
now blocks green, same as setwd()), and the per-paper summary_table's
code_install_packages column.

Deliberately narrower than the issue's own proposed 3-tier traffic light
(green/yellow for commented-out/red for live): confirmed with the
maintainer that only a live call should ever fire the check at all, not a
separate yellow tier for commented-out instances -- which the
comment-stripped-input design already guarantees for free.

highlights.body:
The previous fix (excluding models_posit specifically, see the earlier
commit on this same function) broke again within the same ellmer version
bump: ellmer 0.5.0 added models_update_prices() -- a maintenance utility
that refreshes cached pricing data and returns a plain logical, not a

llm_model_list() used to discover providers. Its boolean result reached

install pulling ellmer 0.5.0 hit this immediately when calling
llm_model_list() (report_app()'s Options tab calls it on startup) -- the
Posit device-code login from before is gone, but the function still fails
outright, just from a different proximate cause. Patching each new
offender as it's discovered (posit, now update_prices) will keep breaking
on the next ellmer release that adds anything else matching "models_.+".

explicit allowlist (.LLM_ALLOWED_PLATFORMS) of the providers metacheck
actually reviews and documents supporting, intersected against whatever
the installed ellmer version exports. A genuinely new provider ellmer adds
in the future is simply not queried until someone deliberately reviews it
and adds it here, rather than being auto-adopted the moment it exists.

provider's results too.

pak::pkg_install of this exact commit): llm_model_list() completes in 5.4s
with no error, posit/update_prices/github all correctly absent from
results.

highlights.body:
fsd_links()/fsd_info() mirror archive-psycharchives.R's shape: list a
study's metadata and file inventory via an open, unauthenticated API,
without downloading anything. Confirmed live 2026-09-09 against a real
study (FSD2653, "Finnish National Election Study 2011"): FSD exposes an
open DDI-C 2.5 XML metadata record per study at
services.fsd.tuni.fi/catalogue/<ID>/DDI/<ID>_eng.xml, no auth needed,
including study title, DOI, an access-restriction statement, and one
fileDscr block per data file (name, format, case/variable counts).

download URI anywhere -- downloading FSD data itself requires Haka
(Finnish higher-education federated login), an Aila account, or a
per-dataset access-application form for most studies, none of which a

item. This is a genuine capability gap in FSD's own API, not an oversight
here (verified: doi.org/10.60686/t-fsd2653's DDI record was fetched and
inspected directly).

urn.fi URN) plus a bare "FSD####" in-text mention; .fsd_study_id() extracts
a canonical study id from any of them, verified against all three live.

INSIDE a .zip via byte-range listing, with no file_url of its own, fetched
through .zip_fetch_members()'s per-member range-request mechanism instead)
was invisible to both size caps entirely. The archive-member block runs
before, and independently of, the per-repo budget loop that enforces
max_file_size/max_download_size for ordinary file_url downloads, and the
code said as much ("Does not touch a row with a real file_url, so this is
purely additive for archive-member rows") without applying any cap of its
own.

paper 10_1111_1365_2435_14173) whose zip-peek listing named several 1-2 GB

despite max_file_size = 100 (MB) and max_download_size = 500 (MB) both set.
data_check then read each multi-GB file in full and classified every
column, taking ~42 minutes for that single paper.

in oversize_skipped for the existing reporting) and a per-ARCHIVE budget
(smallest members first, up to the cap) before fetching. Scoped per archive
rather than per repository -- unifying budgets across the archive-member and
file_url paths would need the two paths merged, which this does not
attempt; this closes the specific gap that let one archive's members bypass

this paper's real member sizes: 8 of 15 members excluded by the per-file

highlights.message: Silence knitr::purl()'s harmless per-chunk stderr spam in code_extract_r()
highlights.body:
A chunk HEADER that references a variable only ever defined by an earlier
CODE chunk (e.g. a chunk option like fig.width=x, set by a preceding chunk)
fails to evaluate under purl()/tangle mode, since tangle mode extracts code
without ever running it. Confirmed live against a real repository in the
Cooper corpus (Zenodo 4721453, OHI-Northeast, documents/methods/
layers_all.Rmd): this one file printed 23 lines of "Error in eval(x, envir
= envir) : object 'x' not found" during a corpus-validation run, yet
knitr::purl() still returned the complete, correctly extracted code (144
lines). This is knitr's own internal per-chunk recovery -- it writes the
caught error straight to the stderr connection (not an R condition; neither
tryCatch(error = ...) nor a message() handler catches it) rather than
raising anything, so one broken chunk header does not abort the rest of the
document. The lines are therefore not a real failure, but they read exactly
like a crash in a long-running corpus log, and a document with many
dynamically-optioned chunks can print this many times over. Redirected via
sink(type = "message") instead, since that is the only thing that catches
output bypassing R's condition system entirely.

Also fixes an incidental bug found in the same function: its two on.exit()
calls lacked add = TRUE, so the second silently replaced the first and the
temp output file was never actually deleted on a normal call (only the
knitr option reset ran).

highlights.message: Fix data_check crash and wasted work in date/datetime column classification
highlights.body:
strptime() (via as.POSIXct's format parser) hard-errors -- rather than
returning NA -- on an input string longer than ~1000 characters (confirmed
live: R's internal strptime buffer is fixed-size). A free-text column (e.g.
an open-ended survey response) routinely has values that long, and
.parse_frac() crashed the entire data_check module the moment such a column
reached it, not just that one column. Confirmed as the exact cause of three
separate corpus-rerun crashes on the same paper (2026-09-03, 2026-09-05,
2026-09-08). Overlong values are now treated as unparseable (NA) instead.

Separately, .parse_frac() is also called for any column whose NAME suggests
a date (e.g. a column literally named "day"), regardless of whether the
column's VALUES are already known to be numeric. A strptime-style format can
never match a bare number, so this always returned 0, just slowly: up to 18
as.POSIXct() passes over the full column. Measured live on a real 331k-row
Darwin Core dataset from the corpus: a numeric "day" column alone cost 2.27s
of an 11.3s total classification pass (~10x every other column). Skipping
straight to 0 for a numeric column changes no result, only the time to
reach it -- confirmed the same file now classifies in 8.9s, with "day" at
0.02s.

highlights.message: Add optional on-disk cache for repo_check's own listing/API calls
highlights.body:
repo_check() gains cache = TRUE (off by default), threaded through every
host it queries with a real API call: Dryad, Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare,
ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, OSF, GitHub, GitLab, and PsychArchives. Each
repository's listing result (what files it has) is now cached separately
from the downloaded file bytes (which repo_cache_dir() already caches).

Root cause: a restart re-issues every listing call from scratch even for a
repository whose files are already fully downloaded. During the Cooper
corpus rerun, 11 restarts x 40+ Dryad listing calls each (2 requests per
dataset) produced 440+ redundant requests against a workload that genuinely
needed a handful -- this repeated re-listing, not the actual download
volume, was what exhausted Dryad's rate limit. Caching the listing makes a
restart free for anything already listed once.

A transient failure (host down, 404, parse error) is never cached -- only a
successfully-listed result is written, via .repo_info_ok()/
.repo_info_list_ok(), so a later restart still retries a genuine miss rather
than replaying a cached failure forever. ResearchBox needed no change: it
has no listing API (listing IS the download), and already reuses a
previously-downloaded archive unconditionally via the existing file-bytes
cache.

highlights.message: docs(changelog): drop the absolute offsets — they do not transfer; keep the gap, which does
highlights.body:
843394a published `char 60080 intact / char 60155 destroyed` from a consumer's pre-fix store.
The labels were right, but the numbers should not have been published at all, and measuring it
here is what showed why:

    consumer's 1.9.57 store   HapMap3 @ 60080   HapMap * @ 60155
    my 1.9.65 re-extraction   HapMap3 @ 60110   HapMap3   @ 60185

SAME PAPER, SAME TWO OCCURRENCES, DIFFERENT ABSOLUTE POSITIONS. An offset is a property of one
extraction's exact text, not of the defect, so a consumer running `grep -ob` against its own
store would meet a discrepancy with an entirely mundane cause -- while already anxious about
corrupted data. Byte and character offsets differ AGAIN within a single file (43 bytes of
multi-byte UTF-8 upstream in that store, so `grep -ob` reports 60096 where python reports
60080), which would force the unit to be stated as well.

WHAT TRANSFERS IS THE GAP, and it is the load-bearing half: the two occurrences are 75 apart,
IDENTICAL IN CHARACTERS AND IN BYTES, measured independently by both parties on two different
extractions. The text between them is a single sentence boundary:

    HapMap3 SNPs. Inclusion in the LD Score regression analysis was limited to

So "same token, same paragraph, 75 apart, one rewritten and one not" survives every way of
measuring it, and that is the sentence a consumer needs. The counts (`HapMap3` = 1,
`HapMap *` = 1 pre-fix) are the other durable part. The offsets were the most fragile thing in
the block and the only part nobody could reproduce.

The general point, worth more than this edit: A NUMBER THAT CANNOT BE REPRODUCED BY THE AUDIENCE
IS NOT EVIDENCE TO THEM, IT IS AN INVITATION TO A CONTRADICTION. Publish the invariant, not the
coordinate.

Raised by the consumer that supplied the original figures, who also corrected their own prose
(they had described character offsets as byte offsets). Verified here rather than relayed.
highlights.author: Gilad Feldman

highlights.message: docs(changelog): the pre-fix half — 2 in the source, 1 destroyed, 75 characters apart
highlights.body:
5036c9a reproduced the POST-fix side from the custody PDF (HapMap3 = 2 at normalization 1.9.65)
and that settled whether the original claim held. It could not show what an AFFECTED file looks
like, because docpluck no longer produces one. The consumer supplied that half from its own
1.9.57 store, with byte offsets and a control this time:

    corpus-text__docpluck-norm@1.9.57.txt  (112,876 B)
      char 60080  INTACT     "...focusing on HapMap3 SNPs. Inclusion in the LD Score regression..."
      char 60155  DESTROYED  "...limited to HapMap * SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF)..."
      HapMap3 = 1     HapMap * = 1     HapMap 3 = 0

Put beside the post-fix measurement the whole picture is there: 2 occurrences in the source, 1
destroyed before the fix, 0 after.

THE TWO SURVIVORS ARE 75 CHARACTERS APART, IN CONSECUTIVE SENTENCES. That is the sharpest
statement of why a single site settles nothing: the same token, the same paragraph, one rewritten
and one not. A scan that stops at the first hit reads whichever it happens to meet, and either
answer is defensible from the evidence it looked at.

ONE PRACTICAL SOFTENING, and it is the consumer's correction to my wording rather than mine: an
intact sibling may sit nearby, so a consumer can SOMETIMES recover the original by scanning.
Re-extraction at 1.9.65+ is the RELIABLE route, not the ONLY one. An intermediate revision of the
notice said "only", which overstates the damage and would send someone re-running a pipeline when
a grep would have answered it.

For the record on the exchange that produced this: their retraction and my re-correction crossed
in flight, so their "STOP, revert 0febe36" arrived after 5036c9a had already reverted it. Both
sides converged on the same reproduced answer independently, which is the useful property of
having measured it rather than argued it.

highlights.message: docs(changelog): withdraw yesterday's correction — I published a consumer's claim without reproducing it
highlights.body:
The paragraph added in 0febe36 said "both forms coexist" is not a general property of the W0k
damage, on a consumer's report that its copy of 10.1038/s41562-024-02076-3 held only the
destroyed form. Its author has withdrawn it. **The error on this side is that I edited a PUBLIC
document on a relayed measurement I had not reproduced** -- and this project's own rule is that a
reviewer's finding is a HYPOTHESIS until a local reproduction confirms it. Two hops, no
verification, and it reached the public CHANGELOG and the notice every consumer is acting on.

REPRODUCED NOW, at the source, which is what should have happened first:

    10.1038/s41562-024-02076-3, re-extracted from the custody PDF at normalization 1.9.65
      HapMap3  = 2       HapMap 3 = 0       HapMap * = 0
        "...focusing on HapMap3 SNPs. Inclusion in the LD Score regression..."
        "...analysis was limited to HapMap3 SNPs with a minor allele frequency..."

    10.1073/pnas.2313604121, same method
      Deposited 3 = 1    Deposited * = 0
        "Deposited 3 December 2022."

Both occurrences of the identifier are `HapMap3` in the source, and the pre-fix pipeline
destroyed exactly ONE of the two. So the ORIGINAL claim was right and is now measured rather than
relayed, and the date shape is independently confirmed rather than taken on trust.

THE RULE RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, and only one half was written down before: a single clean site
cannot clear a document, AND a single destroyed site does not condemn one. Count every
occurrence.

HOW THE WRONG CLAIM WAS MANUFACTURED, because the mechanism is more useful than the correction.
The consumer verified with `grep -c 'HapMap 3'` -- WITH A SPACE -- against an intact form that
has none. They searched for a string that cannot exist, got 0, and read that zero as a finding.
`HapMap 3` returns 0 against a fully intact file; the trap is now demonstrated rather than
predicted, and it fired in the SAME message that flagged the no-space trap to others.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE LESSON. Their 30-file statistics scan carried two-sided controls and held up
completely. The claim that failed was a one-line verification grep, where nobody thinks to plant
a control. Knowing a failure mode by name does not prevent it; a control does, and effort tracks
the ceremony of the check rather than the weight of the conclusion drawn from it.

Nothing else in 0febe36 is affected: the date shape stands (verified above), and the measured
"no published statistic corrupted across 30 files" result stands with its controls intact.

highlights.message: docs(changelog): "both forms coexist" is NOT general, and W0k also destroyed a bare DATE digit
highlights.body:
Two corrections to the 2.4.140 section, both from a consumer's own measurement rather than from
this repo, and both making the picture WORSE in one direction and better in another.

1. THE RECOVERY CLAIM WAS TOO OPTIMISTIC. This file said `10.1038/s41562-024-02076-3` holds both
   `HapMap3 SNPs.` intact and `HapMap *` destroyed, and drew "a single clean site cannot clear a
   document". True of the copy examined here. But in the CONSUMER'S copy at normalization 1.9.57
   the token is destroyed at EVERY occurrence -- `HapMap3` count 0, `HapMap 3` count 0 -- so
   there is nothing in that file to recover from. "Both forms coexist" is a property of one
   extraction, not of the defect. Re-extraction from the source PDF is then the only route, which
   is a materially different instruction to give a consumer.

2. A THIRD SHAPE, WITH A REAL DOI. `10.1073/pnas.2313604121` shipped `Deposited * December 2022.`
   for `Deposited 3 December 2022.` -- a bare day-of-month digit with SPACES ON BOTH SIDES. Every
   example previously recorded (HapMap3, ASL TO3, GRCh3, Material 3, x3) was a digit glued to a
   word or an identifier, so a pattern anchored to that shape misses this class entirely. Verified
   by re-extracting the custody PDF through a service at identity 2.4.141/3f035f5/clean, not by
   pattern-matching. This meets the project's standing rule that a case comes from a real paper
   with the DOI recorded, never from a constructed string.

   Two grep traps follow and are now written down: the intact form is `HapMap3` with NO space, so
   grepping `HapMap 3` returns 0 and reads as a failed fix; and the standalone-digit class needs
   its own pattern.

3. THE REASSURING HALF, AND IT IS MEASURED. Across that consumer's 30-file corpus NO PUBLISHED
   STATISTIC was corrupted. The unambiguous signature is a star sandwiched between digits -- a
   significance star can never sit there -- and it returned 0 sites in 30 files under a TWO-SIDED
   control: planted `12*4` and `0.6*9` caught, planted `0.695***` and `0.34**` ignored, 1,094
   asterisks counted to prove the files were read, and 0 surviving `×`/`✕`/`⨯` glyphs to prove the
   asterisk surface was complete rather than a subset. The damage class is identifiers, names and
   dates -- not statistics.

THEIR PROCESS IS WORTH RECORDING AS MUCH AS THEIR RESULT. Their first scan flagged
`240 participants * 8 items` as corruption and the NEGATIVE control caught it. A later pass
reported "0 corrupted statistics" while its own POSITIVE control was dead -- the planted string
contained no genuine digit-star-digit, so the pattern had never been exercised and that zero was
untested rather than clean. Both are exactly the "a zero is a claim about the instrument" failure
this project keeps re-learning, caught here by controls rather than by luck.

The same consumer independently reproduced this release's "PDF table output is byte-identical"
claim: `flattened_row_count`, `flattened_row_field_keys` and `flattened_row_keys` unchanged
across table extraction 2.4.12 -> 2.4.14 on their PDF fixture.

The consumer notice carries all of the above.

highlights.message: fix(pin): the bump commit carries the frontend mirror, or it does not happen
highlights.body:
`check_app_pin_sync.py --fix` rewrote service/requirements.txt and then staged
that ONE path. frontend/docpluck-pin.json is a committed mirror of the same pin
and was never regenerated or added, so every --fix run pushed a master whose own
suite was red on frontend/src/lib/errors/docpluck-pin.test.ts.

WHY THE MIRROR EXISTS: the documented CLI deploy is `cd frontend && vercel --prod`,
which uploads ONLY frontend/ and therefore cannot read ../service/requirements.txt.
Without a fresh mirror that build falls back to the hand-maintained DOCPLUCK_VERSION
env var -- the 50-day-stale cache-key failure the derivation was built to remove.

IT HAD ALREADY HAPPENED. 54c9a31 bumped the pin to v2.4.138 and stranded the mirror
at 2.4.137. Nobody noticed until a QA session went looking an hour before this
release -- because the failure is SILENT in this repo and lands as red tests in the
app's suite, which this project does not run. Reported by the pdfextractor-65 and
docpluck-ef sessions; VERIFIED HERE AT THE SOURCE before acting on it (line 221 was
the function's only `git add`, and a two-sided grep found 8 hits for "requirements"
against 0 for pin.json/frontend/mirror/sync-pin, so the instrument worked).

THE FIX CALLS THE EXISTING GENERATOR rather than writing the JSON in Python: one
concept, one implementation. A second copy of the mirror format here would drift
from frontend/scripts/sync-docpluck-pin.mjs silently, which is the failure this
project's "ONE CONCEPT, ONE TABLE" rule exists to prevent. A missing `node` is a
HARD FAILURE, never a skip -- skipping is the original defect wearing a green tick,
and the resulting commit would push a red master.

TESTS, watched RED FIRST against the unpatched function and re-verified red after
the third assertion was corrected: 3 failed / 0 passed unpatched, 3 passed patched.
The fixture copies the REAL generator instead of reimplementing it, and the
"both paths staged" test asserts requirements.txt is present FIRST, as a control so
the mirror assertion cannot pass vacuously.

ONE THING WENT WRONG WRITING THEM, recorded because it is this repo's own recurring
trap: the missing-generator test first asked whether the mirror path appeared in
HEAD's file list -- true of the FIXTURE'S base commit, so it failed against correct
code and would have been "fixed" by weakening it. It now compares the HEAD sha,
which is the question that was meant: did this call create a commit at all?

AND THE HARDCODED SIBLING NAME IS GONE. Locating the consumer checkout is now
STRUCTURAL -- the sibling whose service/requirements.txt carries a docpluck pin --
with $DOCPLUCK_APP_REPO and --app-repo as overrides. Two reasons, and the second is
the durable one: this repo is PUBLIC and a hardcoded name published the private
consumer's layout (the public-repo guard blocked the commit that merely MOVED the
literal, which is the gate working); and a name is the more fragile key anyway,
since relocating the checkout would have sent this gate at a path that does not
exist. It returns None rather than a plausible-but-wrong path, so "found nothing"
cannot be misread as "checkout has moved".

Six tests. The resolver's own three are two-sided: a decoy sibling with the right
SHAPE but no pin, sorted FIRST so a resolver that took the first match would fail;
a layout where nothing matches, asserting None rather than a guess; and the env
override. Verified at the REAL call site too -- running the gate resolves the
checkout and reads the pin from origin/master, which a wrong directory could not
do. That run also caught a NameError the refactor introduced (`lib_repo` was still
used further down), which no unit test would have reached.
